title: The Greener Side of Biotechnology

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For a long time people have thought of biotechnology as involving dangerous interference with the genes in food crops. But biotechnology is of course about much more than food production. The first wave of biotech products proved beneficial in the field of medicine, but this has unfortunately been overshadowed by the supposed risks of biotech's second wave, in agriculture. Might its third wave – industrial biotech, also known as green chemistry – resolve biotechnology’s image problem?

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: As with other forms of biotechnology, industrial biotech involves genetic engineering – the production of biological molecules and 'microbes'* with distinctive new properties. What is different in industrial biotech is how these molecules and microbes are then used – to replace chemical processes with biological ones. Whether this is to produce chemicals for other processes, or to create products such as new fuels for vehicles or materials with new properties, there is huge scope to harness biology in order to replace big, dirty chemical factories with cleaner and greener methods of production.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Søren Riisgaard, chief executive of biotechnology company Novozymes, says he imagines a future in which bio-refineries are dotted around the countryside producing fuels and other chemicals from sustainable resources. Novozymes, as its name suggests, has focused its attention on supplying genetically-modified enzymes, that is, biological molecules that help make reactions happen faster, or at lower temperatures. This type of change may sound trivial but it can make the difference between a commercial and a non-commercial process. The company says it has 47% of the market for industrial enzymes, which are used in areas such as detergents, baking and the production of animal foods.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Enzymes are the first choice in industrial biotechnology for carrying out simple chemical conversion processes. But if a more complicated series of reactions is required, or the enzyme in the process is used up during conversion and needs to be recreated, it is time to reach for a microbe. Microbes can accomplish hundreds of chemical tasks at the same time and are able to recreate the enzymes they need.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Assigning a suitable microbe to do a particular job involves starting off with a microbe that can do one part of the job in question, and then convincing the microbe to specialize in that activity. The next stage is to stop the microbe from doing things that are not needed for that particular job, by switching off non-essential genes. The technologists then produce the modified microbes in large numbers and pick out those that are best at the job.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Another company which has been working on industrial biotechnology for years is DSM, based in Heerlen in the Netherlands. DSM started out in the 1980s making enzymes, but in chemical production. Their most recent efforts this time are being used to produce a chemical called succinic acid, which is used to make a wide range of products. The direct chemical process entails making succinic acid from crude oil or natural gas. But biological alternatives are now being developed using sugar beet. After a successful pilot biotechnological phase, the next stage is a fermentation factory in Leeuwarden, which will show whether a much bigger commercial operation will follow. The company says that as well as using biologically derived starch rather than fossil fuels for making succinic acid, the process it now uses also requires 40% less energy and produces fewer carbon dioxide emissions.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Those who support industrial biotechnology are optimistic that it can avoid the drawbacks that hindered the adoption of biotech crops, which have been criticised by their opponents as unnatural and potentially dangerous. For one thing, while crops such as genetically modified tomatoes, for example, are purchased by consumers straight away, industrial-biotech products are not – they go on to be used for industrial purposes. And instead of replacing natural products with biogenetic alternatives, as in agriculture, industrial biotechnology generally replaces fossil fuels with greener biological alternatives. Surely that should make it easier to convince people of its benefits, and hence to rehabilitate the notion of biotechnology more widely?

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: But there are still some difficult ethical questions. Using food crops like maize as raw materials to make biofuel is already hugely controversial because of its impact on food prices. And even growing non-food crops for industrial use is problematic, because this can reduce the amount of land that can be used for food production. It has also been suggested that raw materials could be grown on land which is unsuitable for food production. This is true, but it could have knock-on effects on biodiversity, affecting the habitats of native plant and animal species. The use of agricultural waste is less controversial. There are plentiful supplies, and it can be converted into other chemicals (including fuels). But perhaps the most promising approach for advocates of biotechnology's third wave is to emphasize the potential for a greener chemicals industry which could create employment for people living in isolated places far from towns and cities.

groups.title: Arguments for and against industrial biotechnology
content: The supporters of industrial biotechnology feel it has fewer drawbacks than agricultural biotechnology. For example, as products are not sold directly to {{22}} , industrial biotechnology also offers more acceptable alternatives to fossil fuels.

But there are still problems associated with industrial biotechnology. Using food crops for biofuel raises food prices, and growing non food crops means less {{23}} is available for growing food. Even if non-food crops are grown in areas unsuitable for food production, this could affect the habitats of plants and animals, thus reducing {{24}} . People are not so concerned about the use of {{25}} for chemical production, since this is freely available.
However, a very important argument in favour of industrial biotechnology is that it could give {{26}} to inhabitants of remote rural areas.
